title: Do these two numbers share any prime, or are they co-prime?
description: The different primes of each number are listed and the two lists are compared. Keeko doubts this and says both have three primes so they must share one.
teaching_notes: One idea: sharing a prime depends on which primes appear, not on how many. Watch for students who compare the count of primes instead of the primes themselves.

source: Consider 242 and 195. Their prime factorisations are 242 = 2
video_script.why: The child sees that two numbers are co-prime when the lists of their different primes share nothing, whatever the counts of primes.
video_script.substitution: the book's own numbers, two hundred and forty two and one hundred and ninety five
video_script.anchor: the rows of primes of two hundred and forty two and of one hundred and ninety five, with their lists of different primes beside them
video_script.wrong_answer: both have three primes so they must share one
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko counts three primes in each row and thinks that makes them share a prime.
video_script.payoff_line: Two hundred and forty two and one hundred and ninety five are co-prime

final_answer.spoken: two hundred and forty two and one hundred and ninety five are co-prime

maths_rules: no prime is in both lists, so 242 and 195 are co-prime
each row has three primes written, but how many primes there are does not decide sharing

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks both have three primes so they must share one.
<bookmark mark='lists'/>But counting the primes tells us nothing, because sharing depends on which primes appear.
<bookmark mark='strike'/>We write the different primes of each number and compare the two lists.
